title: planning: one flow from business request to release, ports for task and spec, reason to exist in README
description:
Intent (settled with the person in grilling, 2026-10-11/12): one planning flow for a solo developer who ships CLIs, desktop apps, component libraries and Claude marketplaces, where the person plays product owner, tech lead and reviewer and the agent drafts everything. Modelled on Anthropic's AI-native SDLC playbook (intent -> spec -> plan -> PR), with plan.md replaced by spec plus tasks.md.

Flow and decisions:
1. Business request: the first messages of a conversation, before an intent exists. Not stored apart; the session archive holds it.
2. Grilling (product owner level: what it does, how it behaves, how it looks) produces the intent of the work, written into a br epic with its acceptance criteria. Gate: the person's yes.
3. Plan (tech lead level): the epic is split into pieces; each piece gets one br task under the epic and its own OpenSpec change (proposal, spec deltas, design: where things go, basic abstractions). The task is created with the spec, never before. Gate: the person's yes to the spec.
4. tasks.md of the change is the developer's local breakdown of that one task (files, order, proof); subtasks never go into br. Gate: the person's yes before code.
5. Apply, review through the review agent, push. Archive closes the change's task.
6. Every epic has acceptance criteria and a final test-it task that runs the real path end to end. The epic closes only when all its tasks are done, every acceptance criterion holds, the test-it task passed, and the work is pushed after review.
7. A fix: a commit only (its why in the message); no epic, task or spec.
8. Wayfinder is merged into the epic: open decisions of large work are child tasks of kind decision, settled by grilling. The wayfinder skill is removed.
9. Ports, not tools: plan names the roles task and spec, never br or OpenSpec. The task port is a new plug-in qsm-tasks (the task-tool skill leaves qsm-essentials, the br install leaves qsm-plan); the spec port is qsm-openspec. qsm-plan requires both as declared dependencies with reasons (AGENTS.md, Architecture rule 2); no fallback.
10. Reason to exist: a project's or plugin's permanent reason for existing becomes the first README section "## Why it exists", five sentences at most, held by a validate gate. INTENT.md files are removed. "Intent" now means only the intent of a piece of work, in its epic.
11. No fallbacks, compatibility or history (rules/implementation.md, "One path").

Acceptance criteria:
- qsm-plan's skills and spec describe steps 1-8 and name ports only; the wayfinder skill is gone.
- qsm-tasks exists with the task skill rewritten to this model, the br install and a doctor; qsm-essentials and qsm-plan no longer hold either.
- qsm-openspec creates the change's br task with the spec and treats tasks.md as the local breakdown.
- Every plugin and the root README open with "## Why it exists" (<= 5 sentences, gate enforced); no INTENT.md is left; AGENTS.md, the generated instructions, add-plugin and the console read the new place.
- The console shows each plugin's reason to exist, its dependencies with their reasons, and the epics and tasks that name it.
- A test-it run: a fresh session plans one small real feature through the whole flow and every gate asks.

title: grilling: what qsm-ccr IS — CCR vs ccx scope, provider set, config surface
description:
GRILLING TICKET. Run with the user, one session, before any qsm-ccr file exists. The parent
qsm-brain-collapse-map-g58.10 already carries ten settled facts from the 2026-08-28 build session —
do not relearn them and do not re-decide them. This ticket settles only what that session left open.

The parent's comment of 2026-08-29 names three open questions. They are restated here with the
reason each one changes the tool's shape.

1. CCR vs ccx — what is the deliverable?
   Two things were built by hand on 2026-08-28: the claude-code-router daemon with its sqlite
   config, and ~/.zsh-functions/ccx.sh, a shell function that launches Claude Code against that
   daemon with per-model context and tier envs. They are separable. A tool that sets up only the
   daemon is useful to anyone; a tool that also ships ccx.sh assumes zsh and one person's shell
   layout. Decide whether qsm-ccr owns one, the other, or both behind a flag.
   WHY it changes the shape: if ccx.sh is in scope, the tool needs a shell-integration surface and
   a machine-local install path, which is the whole of sibling ticket "where does ccx.sh land".

2. Which providers ship configured, and which are documented only?
   Settled: codex-api via `codex login` OAuth is the anchor provider. Also present on the built
   machine: OpenRouter and Zen as plain api_key entries, keys through qsm-secret. Decide whether
   the installer writes those two provider rows (requiring a secret to exist at install time), or
   whether it writes only codex-api and documents the rest.
   WHY it changes the shape: writing them means the installer must handle "secret not present yet"
   as a normal path, not an error, or the install is not idempotent on a fresh machine.

3. What is the config surface the user edits?
   The live config is a JSON blob inside sqlite (~/.claude-code-router/config.sqlite, table
   app_config, key 'default', column value_json) — NOT a file the user can edit. Decide whether
   qsm-ccr owns a neutral source-of-truth file it renders into sqlite, or whether it only writes
   sqlite once and then gets out of the way.
   WHY it changes the shape: a rendered config means the tool must handle drift (the daemon
   rewrites parts of that blob on start), which is a different tool from a one-shot writer.

Also settle, because the parent lists them as facts without deciding their scope:

4. Does the tool ship a doctor verb, and what does it assert? Candidate assertions from the build
   session: daemon reachable on its port, api_keys row present and extracted to a 0600 file,
   profile scope is 'ccr' and enabled=false, CUSTOM_ROUTER_PATH points at an existing file,
   `codex debug models` returns the expected model list.

5. What is explicitly OUT? Already recorded as out on the parent: Anthropic subscription OAuth
   through CCR (rejected, ban risk), and new harnesses. Confirm nothing else joins that list.

OUTPUT of this ticket: the settled answers written back onto qsm-brain-collapse-map-g58.10 as a
comment, then a rung-2 spec through the spec-propose skill. This ticket does not write code and does
not write the spec — it produces the decisions the spec needs.
acceptance_criteria: All five questions answered by the user and written back as a comment on qsm-brain-collapse-map-g58.10, each answer carrying its reason. Nothing from the parent's ten settled facts is re-decided. No code written. The rung-2 spec-propose run is unblocked, and this issue names the exact scope sentence the spec starts from.

title: decision: how the scope='ccr' guard is set before the daemon ever starts
description:
DECISION TICKET. The single highest-cost mistake found in the 2026-08-28 build session, recorded on
the parent as settled fact (4):

  "CRITICAL: profile.profiles[agent=claude-code] ships scope='global' and REWRITES
  ~/.claude/settings.json env on every daemon start — must set scope='ccr' + enabled=false BEFORE
  first daemon start (this broke the user's live sessions 3x)"

Read that failure mode plainly, because it decides the tool's whole install order. claude-code-router
ships a profile whose scope is 'global'. When the daemon starts, that profile writes environment
variables into the user's ~/.claude/settings.json. Any Claude Code session already running, or
started later, picks up those variables and routes through the daemon whether or not the user asked
for it. On 2026-08-28 this happened three times before the cause was found.

So the install has an ordering constraint that a normal installer does not have: the config must be
correct BEFORE the daemon is ever started, including the very first start that `bun add -g` or a
first `ccr` invocation might trigger. An installer that starts the daemon to create the config, then
fixes the config, has already caused the damage.

What must be decided:

1. How does the installer write the sqlite config without starting the daemon?
   The config lives at ~/.claude-code-router/config.sqlite, table app_config, key 'default', column
   value_json. If that file does not exist before first start, the installer has to create the
   schema itself, which couples qsm-ccr to a schema it does not own and which upstream may change.
   The alternative is to let the daemon create it, kill the daemon, patch, restart — which accepts
   one window where settings.json is rewritten. Neither option is free. Pick one and record why.

2. What proves the guard held?
   Decide the check that runs after install and after every daemon start: read
   profile.profiles[agent=claude-code].scope and .enabled out of the blob and assert 'ccr' /
   false. Decide whether that check also belongs in a doctor verb, and whether it should refuse to
   report success while ~/.claude/settings.json contains daemon-injected env.

3. What does the tool do when it finds the damage already done?
   A machine where this already fired has ANTHROPIC_* env in ~/.claude/settings.json that the user
   did not put there. Decide whether qsm-ccr removes it, reports it, or refuses to proceed. Removing
   another tool's writes from the user's settings file is destructive and needs an explicit
   decision, not a default.

WHY this is a separate ticket from the grilling ticket: the grilling ticket settles what the tool
IS. This settles a named, measured failure that any shape of the tool has to survive, and its answer
constrains install ordering, which is the first thing the spec has to state.
acceptance_criteria: Three answers recorded on this issue with reasons: (1) how the sqlite config is written without a daemon start, or which damage window is accepted and why; (2) the exact assertion that proves the guard held, and where it runs; (3) what the tool does on a machine where settings.json already carries daemon-injected env — remove, report, or refuse. The install ordering constraint is stated in one sentence the spec can quote verbatim.

title: decision: where ccx.sh lands without hardcoding a machine path, and which shells it serves
description:
DECISION TICKET. Only in play if the grilling ticket puts ccx.sh in scope.

Settled fact (8) on the parent describes what was built by hand on 2026-08-28:

  "~/.zsh-functions/ccx.sh: default sol, shorthand args, per-model CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS,
  tier envs haiku->mini sonnet->terra opus->sol (subagent plumbing only), daemon ensure via port
  probe"

Every part of that path is machine-specific. `~/.zsh-functions/` is one person's zsh layout. Iron
Law 11 and docs/content-layers.md keep concrete machine paths out of this public repository, so the
installer cannot contain that string.

What must be decided:

1. How does the installer learn where shell functions go?
   Candidates, none picked: an environment variable the user sets; a value in the qsm setup state
   file (~/.config/qsm/setup.json, already the canonical setup state per adapters/claude/CLAUDE.md);
   a prompt at install time; or XDG-style detection with a documented default. Each has a different
   idempotency story — a prompt is not idempotent in a scripted install, and detection is not
   idempotent across shells.

2. Which shells are supported?
   The built artefact is zsh. The repository already has qsm-langdev-fish, qsm-langdev-zsh and
   qsm-langdev-shell, so a fish user is a real case here. Decide whether qsm-ccr ships one POSIX
   function sourced by both, per-shell variants, or zsh only with the limitation stated in
   INSTALL.md.

3. Is the model-to-tier mapping config or code?
   Fact (8) hardcodes haiku->mini, sonnet->terra, opus->sol, and fact (7) lists the codex-api model
   set (gpt-5.6-sol/luna/terra at 368k ctx, gpt-5.5, gpt-5.4, gpt-5.4-mini at 256k, gpt-reserve,
   codex-auto-review at 272k). That model list is upstream's and will change. A hardcoded mapping in
   the shell function drifts silently the first time a model is renamed. Decide whether the mapping
   lives in the tool's own config, is derived from `codex debug models` at install time, or is
   accepted as hardcoded with a doctor check that flags a missing model.

4. Does the tool own uninstall?
   A shell function installed into a user's dotfiles is something the tool wrote into a file it does
   not own. Decide whether qsm-ccr removes it on uninstall, and if so how it identifies its own
   lines.

Note for whoever picks this up: fact (8) says the tier envs are "subagent plumbing only". That is a
constraint on what the mapping is FOR, not a suggestion — the tiers exist so dispatched subagents
land on the right model, not so the human types a tier name.
acceptance_criteria: Four answers recorded with reasons: shell-function install location mechanism, supported shells, whether the model-to-tier mapping is config or code, and uninstall ownership. No concrete machine path appears in any proposed source file. The answer is consistent with whatever the grilling ticket decided about ccx being in scope — if ccx is out of scope, this issue is closed as not-applicable with that reason.

title: decision: the auto permission classifier's ~40k-per-decision cost — in scope, documented, or ignored
description:
DECISION TICKET. Settled fact (9) on the parent, recorded without a scope decision:

  "auto permission classifier = separate Sonnet-5-tier call through same base URL (~40k input/
  decision — quota cost)"

Read what that measures. When Claude Code runs in auto-permission mode against the router, each
permission decision costs a separate model call carrying roughly 40k input tokens. Through a
metered provider that is a per-decision bill, and a long session makes many decisions.

What must be decided:

1. In scope for qsm-ccr at all?
   The classifier is Claude Code behaviour, not router behaviour. qsm-ccr may have nothing to do
   with it beyond warning that it exists. Decide whether the tool touches it, documents it, or
   ignores it.

2. If documented — where does the warning belong so it is read before the bill arrives?
   Candidates: tools/qsm-ccr/USAGE.md (a reader pulls it on demand, so it may be read too late), or
   the doctor output (read at setup time, which is when the decision is made).

3. Is there a cheaper routing for it?
   The classifier call goes through the same base URL as everything else, so it lands on whatever
   the default model is. Fact (7) lists gpt-5.4-mini at 256k context as the cheapest model on
   codex-api. Whether the classifier CAN be pointed at a cheaper model is unverified — it was
   observed, not tested. Decide whether to test it, and record the answer either way.

Priority is low because nothing is blocked on it: the tool ships without an answer, the user simply
does not learn the cost until they see it. It is filed because "measured once, never written down"
is how a known cost becomes a surprise six months later.
acceptance_criteria: Recorded on this issue: whether qsm-ccr touches, documents, or ignores the classifier; if documented, which surface carries the warning and why that surface is read in time; and whether pointing the classifier at a cheaper model was tested, with the result either way. An untested claim is labelled unverified, never stated as fact.

description:
Source: Orfeus.Persons ATH-1644 session, 2026-09-01. One RabbitMQ queue-cleanup list was
restructured FIVE times. Every restructure was the user tearing out a layer the model had added
without being asked, and every layer had been defended in prose before being removed.

WHAT THE USER ACTUALLY ASKED FOR, unchanged from the start:
  "the function gets a list of queues, and for each you say whether to keep the data or not, in the
   end they all get deleted, easy. What are you overcomplicating?"

WHAT THE MODEL BUILT INSTEAD, in order, each removed by the user:
  1. `KeepData` set per GROUP in a generator, not per queue. User: "where is the per-queue info?
     What if I wanted PidChange to keep data but OperationResult not?"
  2. `queue with { KeepData = false }` overriding the declared per-item value in code. User:
     "nothing should be overridden, the per-queue setting IS the setting."
  3. `QueueStatus { Live, Retired }` enum, invented so one table could answer two questions. The
     second question ("what does Wolverine listen on?") already had a source the model had itself
     flagged as duplicated a day earlier and then ignored.
  4. `HasLegacySidecarDelayQueues` flag, so a generator could guess names that should have been
     written out.
  5. Flat table with context as a column, written AFTER the user had said the switch was better.
     User: "NENENENEN, the switch was better."
  6. Required `Reason` field, defended twice as auditability. User: "log that you are deleting
     queue X. I don't need a reason."

RESULT AFTER THE USER'S VERSION WON: two files went 475 -> 335 lines, six members deleted, all
1261 tests still green. The simpler design was also the CORRECT one — the layered version had a
data-loss bug the flat one cannot express.

THE USER'S SUMMARY: "you are adding terrible mess there, really terrible."

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THIS SESSION: the model's own instruction file opens with "Fight complexity"
and "Every addition needs a reason or a showcase that proves the lack." Six additions, zero
showcases. Each was justified by an imagined future requirement, not a demonstrated present one.

Candidate rule material for the marketplace instruction set.
acceptance_criteria:
The pattern is stated as a rule the model can apply mid-task, not just described.
The rule distinguishes 'the user asked for a knob' from 'I imagined a knob would be wanted'.
The rule names the tell: defending a structure in prose before anyone has questioned it.

title: A structure invented so one table can answer two questions
description:
`QueueStatus { Live, Retired }` existed only so a single table could say both 'this is mine and
running' and 'I stopped declaring this'. The second fact already had an owner —
`WolverineExtensions.PidQueuesByContext` — which the model had itself identified as duplicated
earlier in the same session and then quietly rebuilt a second copy of.

The user's question was the fix: "why would it need a second list? The function gets a list of
queues... easy." Deleting the enum and reading the existing source removed the enum, the record it
lived on, a helper, and a whole test.

TELL: a field that exists to disambiguate two meanings inside one container usually means the
container is serving two callers who should each have their own input.
acceptance_criteria:
Rule states: before adding a discriminator field, name the two questions and check whether the
second already has a source in the codebase.

title: Fabricated rows presented as a verified inventory
description:
The model wrote a table documented as 'exactly as it appears on the broker, readable line by line
against the broker's own queue list' and filled 21 of its rows with queue names that have never
existed on any broker: `Delay.First/Next.PersonsService.<NC>.Pid.*` and `DLQ.*.ManualReview`.

The user caught it from a screenshot: "in RabbitMQ these queues do NOT have the context in their
name, you put it there."

Verification the model should have run BEFORE writing the rows, and ran only after being told:
`git log` over every revision of the Sidecar bus config — a PID queue appears in NONE of the seven.
So Sidecar never built a retry-delay pair for one, and ManualReview never had a listener so
Wolverine never gave it a dead-letter queue.

Worse: the model had twice ASSERTED to the user that those queues were 'leftovers from before the
ATH-658 migration'. They were never created at all. A claim inherited from an old code comment was
repeated as established fact, and a bead plus a documentation paragraph were built on it.

TELL: describing an artefact as 'the literal inventory' while any row in it is inferred rather than
observed.
acceptance_criteria:
Rule states: a table documented as an inventory of a live system must have every row observed,
and the observation named. An inferred row is either verified or left out.
Rule states: a fact read from a code comment is a lead, not evidence.

title: Arguing from a fragment the user was never shown
description:
Twice the user said 'I still don't see X in the list' about rows that were present. Both times the
model had pasted only one arm of a three-arm switch into the chat and then reasoned about the whole.
The second time the model started rewriting the structure before checking the file, and only then
found the rows at lines 172-175.

Cost: one unnecessary restructure, and a user reasonably concluding the code was wrong.

TELL: answering 'is X in there?' from memory of what was written rather than from the file.
acceptance_criteria:
Rule states: when the user reports something missing, read the file before agreeing or rewriting.
Rule states: when showing a repetitive structure, show enough that the user can see what is NOT in
the part shown, or say explicitly what was elided.

title: The user's evidence outperformed the model's reasoning three times
description:
Not a failure to fix — a signal about where to spend effort. Three of the session's most valuable
findings came from the user pasting a screenshot or a log, and each overturned something the model
had asserted:

1. A production log line showed the delete had never worked, on any broker, because quorum queues
   refuse a conditional delete outright. The model had reasoned about which of two failure modes it
   was and both guesses were wrong.
2. A broker screenshot showed the ManualReview queues held zero messages. The model had told the
   user twice they were 'permanently non-empty', from an old comment.
3. A broker screenshot showed which queue names really exist, exposing the fabricated rows above.

An external review agent also reproduced a real data-loss bug against a live broker that no amount
of reading had surfaced.

TELL: a claim about the state of a running system that has not been read from that system.
acceptance_criteria:
Rule states: for any claim about a live system's state, either measure it or label it as an
assumption in the same sentence.

title: Rewrite: one Claude marketplace, MVP pass 1
description:
Rewrite qsm-marketplace as ONE Claude marketplace: every capability is one plugin that carries its
code, its CLI, its skills, its hooks and its docs together. No tools/, no adapters/. Decided
2026-09-10 with the user, in a grilling round of 13 questions; nothing below is open.

THE USER'S SCOPE, quoted: "Celkove mene docs, mene tests, mene textu. Takze idealne u kazde veci
vzit co tak generarly asi mela delat, a udelat minimal MVP te veci, to bude first pass. Cely
marketplace, no tests, no docs, super simple prompts, MVPs." Docs clarified: must-have docs stay
(README, INSTALL + USAGE for a plugin with a bin, specs), everything explanatory or historical goes.
Specs clarified: EVERY plugin gets openspec/specs in phase 0, written by agents as "super simple MVP
feature-full" specs from the old plugin, and the build follows the spec plus the old plugin as
reference.

SETTLED DECISIONS
1. Re-author, not git mv: each plugin is written again with the old tree as reference; every file
   is reviewed. No test is carried over; pass 1 has no tests. Behaviour tests come in pass 2, per
   plugin, once the MVP shows which behaviour deserves one.
2. Layout: repo root is the marketplace. `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` at root, plugins under
   `plugins/<name>/`. A plugin holds `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, `qsm.json` (bin + commands, only
   when it ships a CLI), `lib/`, `scripts/`, `skills/`, `agents/`, `commands/`, `hooks/`, `openspec/`,
   `README.md`, and `INSTALL.md` + `USAGE.md` only when it ships a bin. The old rule "root plugins/
   is not live source" is inverted: plugins/ IS the source.
3. Shared code lives in root `lib/` outside every plugin: install-contract and the hook build
   helper, nothing else in pass 1 (test helpers do not move, there are no tests). A plugin never
   imports from another plugin; root lib/ is layer 0, plugins/ layer 1. Claude docs describe plugins
   as self-contained and have no sharing convention; this works because our scripts run from the
   repo and hooks are compiled binaries with imports baked in.
4. Language plugins qsm-langdev-{ts,py,dotnet,shell,zsh,fish} stay separate plugins, skills only,
   each declaring `qsm.requires: ["qsm-langdev"]` so the tool installs first and a project adds
   only its languages. Per-language dev notes land there in pass 2.
5. Drops: qsm-cloakbrowser, qsm-skyvern, qsm-stagehand (parked) are not rewritten. qsm-lsp-adapter
   (empty), qsm-claude-lsp-adapter and qsm-csharp-lsp merge into ONE plugin `qsm-lsp`. Any further
   drop: the user closes that plugin's spec bead with the reason; that is the inventory.
6. Prompts: SKILL.md at most 8 KB, one file per skill, one file per agent, no `references/`
   directories in pass 1. Iron Law 5's 48 KB cap becomes 8 KB for skills and agents.
7. Gates in the rewrite worktree: `.qsm-langdev/gates.json` selects `secrets` and `entropy` only,
   until qsm-langdev and qsm-sentrux are rebuilt; then their gates return.
8. Provisioning: branch `rewrite` in a worktree, main frozen except hotfixes, beads DB shared from
   the main checkout (verified: `br list` from a worktree sees the same 102 open issues). One bead
   per plugin per phase; the USER closes a build bead after review, never the agent.
9. The sentrux fork patch (tools/qsm-sentrux/sentrux-0.5.7-qsm.patch, 14 files) is carried byte
   for byte: it is upstream's code plus about 60 lines of ours, not ours to simplify.
10. Workers: sonnet subagents, one plugin per dispatch, in the rewrite worktree; haiku only for
    quick doc writes. The orchestrator reviews before the user does.

PHASES
- Phase 0 (specs): one bead per plugin. Read the old plugin (tools/<name> and
  adapters/claude/modules/<name> on main), write plugins/<name>/openspec/specs as a super simple MVP
  feature-full spec: what it does, its verbs/skills/hooks, its failure behaviour. Nothing about how.
  The user approves each spec by closing the bead.
- Phase 1 (foundation): worktree, wipe, survivors, root lib/, marketplace.json, gates.json,
  AGENTS.md v2, rules.toml, validators. Details in its bead.
- Phase 2 (build): one bead per plugin, depends on its spec bead and on the foundation bead;
  qsm-langdev-* also on qsm-langdev. Acceptance is in each bead.
- Phase 3 (parity + merge): every kept surface installs and runs once by hand, `bun run validate`
  green, gates back on, merge rewrite into main, re-add the marketplace to Claude (its root moved).

START HERE, in a fresh session:
  git -C ~/Projects/qsm-marketplace worktree add -b rewrite ~/Projects/qsm-marketplace.rewrite main
  cd ~/Projects/qsm-marketplace.rewrite
Then take the Phase 0 beads. Disable the user-scope qsm-langdev and qsm-sentrux plugins for that
session: on a wiped tree their stop hooks find no profile and log noise. Re-enable when rebuilt.

WHAT THE WIPE KEEPS (root of the worktree): .git, .beads/ (issues.jsonl is tracked and shared,
never delete it), .gitleaks.toml and .secrets.baseline (the two kept gates fail without them),
mise.toml, .gitignore, .claude/ (project settings, commands, skills), .qsm-langdev/gates.json
rewritten to the two gates. Everything else is deleted in the first commit and rebuilt.

THIRTY-ODD PLUGINS ARE THIN WRAPPERS: 20 to 100 lines of code and 200 to 450 lines of prose that
restate the upstream manual, the violation AGENTS.md already names. Their MVP is plugin.json,
qsm.json when they wrap a binary, one README paragraph with the install command and our caveats.
Do not rewrite 400 lines of docs into 300.
